raw_record.support_text: A cited observational case series of paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose patients treated with standard care, acetylcysteine and fomepizole is discussed, in which the patients were described as 'consecutive with high risk factors' and hepatotoxicity/liver injury was the outcome of interest. The letter disputes claims that fomepizole prevented hepatotoxicity, noting that in several of the 14 patients liver injury may have already peaked or even increased after fomepizole was started, and that nine of the patients treated with acetylcysteine within 8 h were only at low-to-moderate risk of developing hepatotoxicity.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Overdose setting; case series of paracetamol-poisoned patients, several treated with haemodialysis (case 7) or with ALT/AST not measured at the time of fomepizole administration, complicating interpretation; most received acetylcysteine within 8 h.
raw_record.extra_details: Fourteen consecutive cases (six previously published); risk assessed via the paracetamol-aminotransferase multiplication product (>10,000 = high risk in five of fourteen); ALT/AST activities not measured at fomepizole administration; patients described with 'severe paracetamol poisoning' and hepatotoxicity risk; letter authors note porcine/rodent experimental evidence for fomepizole prevention of liver injury, but question efficacy and safety claims due to lack of a formalized protocol and variable fomepizole dosing (single dose 9/14) and timing (6 h in six patients, ≥24 h in four).

raw_record.support_text: The paper reports that hepatotoxicity has not been detected in any of the rimegepant trials to date (acute migraine studies 301, 302, 303, the preventive study NCT03732638, and the long-term study 201), noting that hepatic enzyme elevations observed during the preventive trial (four patients on rimegepant and two on placebo with alanine aminotransferase >3-fold the upper limit of normal) were not considered hepatotoxicity. In the acute-treatment RCTs the drug was tolerated with no hepatotoxicity found.
raw_record.extra_details: Explicit negative: hepatotoxicity not detected in rimegepant 75 mg acute-treatment (studies 301/302/303), preventive (NCT03732638, 75 mg every other day for 12 weeks), and long-term acute-use (study 201) trials in migraine patients. In the preventive study, four patients on the active drug and two on placebo had an alanine aminotransferase increase >3-fold the upper limit of normal, which the authors did not characterize as DILI/hepatotoxicity. In contrast with first-generation gepants, no hepatotoxicity was found.

raw_record.support_text: The paper states that after clinical investigation in thousands of patients (over 24,000 evaluated in completed phase-II and III trials), rivaroxaban appears to have no significant hepatotoxicity, with a bleeding risk comparable to other conventional anticoagulants. It also describes a relatively safe pharmacodynamic profile with respect to bleeding risk and hepatotoxicity in the context of its development plan.
raw_record.extra_details: Explicit negative conclusion: rivaroxaban appears to have no significant hepatotoxicity after evaluation in over 24,000 patients (12,000 predominantly post-operative orthopedic patients) in completed phase II and III trials for thromboprophylaxis and treatment of DVT. Daily dose range 5-20 mg, with 10 mg once daily described as optimal; partially renally cleared, requiring dose adjustment in grade-III chronic kidney disease and not studied below creatinine clearance of 30 ml/min; metabolism affected by potent CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole and clarithromycin. No dose adjustment required for body weight, no clinically significant interaction with aspirin.

raw_record.support_text: A case series described one boy and one girl (median age 15 years) who developed valproic acid-induced acute liver failure. One patient was treated with carnitine 30 mg/kg but died, while the other died before receiving any treatment [38]. This attributes acute liver failure to valproic acid therapy in a paediatric population.
raw_record.extra_details: Both patients with valproic acid-induced acute liver failure died; one had received carnitine 30 mg/kg prior to death while the other died before any treatment; source reference [38].

condition_text: Neonates (5–182 days of age and intensive-care newborns) receiving recommended therapeutic intravenous doses; no pre-existing definable population restriction beyond the pediatric/neonatal setting.

raw_record.support_text: In a retrospective study in 149 neonates (5–182 days of age), intravenous paracetamol (initial dose of 20 mg/kg, then 10 mg/kg at intervals of 6, 8 or 12 hours depending on gestational age) was not associated with hepatotoxicity, with no changes in hepatic enzyme profiles during treatment and up to 2 days after the last dose. Similarly, a safety and pharmacokinetic study in 50 intensive-care neonates given multiple recommended intravenous paracetamol doses found no hepatotoxicity based on liver function tests (ALT, ALP and γ-glutamyl transferase).
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Neonates (5–182 days of age and intensive-care newborns) receiving recommended therapeutic intravenous doses; no pre-existing definable population restriction beyond the pediatric/neonatal setting.
raw_record.extra_details: Retrospective study (n=149 neonates, initial IV dose 20 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg every 6, 8 or 12 h for GA >36, 31–36 and <31 weeks respectively) showed no changes in hepatic enzyme profiles during treatment and up to 2 days after the last dose; safety/pharmacokinetic study (n=50 ICU neonates) showed no hepatotoxicity by ALT, ALP and γ-glutamyl transferase. Study references [7] and [36]. Also stated overall that single and multiple doses of IV paracetamol 15 mg/kg in paediatric patients had a similar safety profile to adults.

raw_record.support_text: Flupirtin (Flupirtine) is reported in association with hepatotoxicity: Puls et al. [34] published five cases of severe liver damage and one case of acute liver failure requiring transplantation in conceivable connection with flupirtine. The liver damage became manifest three weeks to 24 months (median 4 months) after starting flupirtine. Causality was adjudicated by RUCAM as probable in four cases and highly probable in the remaining two cases. During follow-up of 5–25 months (average 16, median 9 months), the liver injury was reversible in five of the six cases.
raw_record.extra_details: Reported by Puls et al. (reference [34]): five cases of severe liver damage and one case of acute liver failure requiring liver transplantation; detailed histological assessment of liver biopsies from five patients. Onset 3 weeks to 24 months (median 4 months) after flupirtine initiation; RUCAM causality: probable in 4 cases, highly probable in 2 cases. Follow-up 5–25 months (average 16, median 9); injury reversible in 5 of 6 cases. Medically indicated chronic pain analgesic use.

raw_record.support_text: The discussion describes ramipril-associated hepatotoxicity in three patients. The first patient on 2 mg/day for 5 months had jaundice, pruritis, slight increases in serum alkaline phosphatase, AST and ALT, portal triad dilatation, moderate mononuclear cell infiltration, septal fibrosis, duct proliferation and zone 1 hepatocellular necrosis; the second on 10 mg/day for 6 weeks had jaundice, pruritis and enzyme increases (more prominent for alkaline phosphatase) with portal triad dilatation and moderate fibrosis; the third on 2.5 mg/day for 6 weeks had AST and ALT increases with hepatitis evidence on histopathology.
raw_record.extra_details: Three patients cited as reference [17]: doses of 2 mg/day (5 months), 10 mg/day (6 weeks) and 2.5 mg/day (6 weeks). Features included jaundice, pruritis, increases in serum alkaline phosphatase, AST and ALT (alkaline phosphatase more prominent in patient 2), portal triad dilatation, mononuclear cell infiltration, septal fibrosis, ductus proliferation and zone 1 hepatocellular necrosis (patient 1); patient 3 had hepatitis evidence on histopathology.

raw_record.support_text: Cases of acute liver failure consistent with paracetamol (acetaminophen) hepatotoxicity were observed in patients who received isoniazid with therapeutic doses of paracetamol. It is suggested that induction of cytochrome P450 2E1 by isoniazid may increase production of the toxic metabolites of paracetamol.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Patients were concurrently receiving isoniazid; paracetamol was given at therapeutic doses.
raw_record.extra_details: Mechanistic suggestion: isoniazid induction of cytochrome P450 2E1 may increase production of paracetamol toxic metabolites. References [53,54].
